candidate.answerReason: Exactly four unordered six-number sets satisfy the logarithm condition. They are {1,5,10,25,u,v}, with u in {2,20} and v in {4,40}. Under the usual fair-lottery model, conditioning on this property leaves four equally likely winning sets.

methods.label: Balance the powers of 2 and 5
methods.explanation:
Use the usual lottery model in which every unordered set of six different numbers is equally likely to win. We need to count the sets that satisfy the extra information about the winning ticket.

The sum of the logarithms is the logarithm of the product. Thus the condition says that the six numbers have product \(10^k=2^k5^k\) for an integer \(k\ge0\). No selected number can contain a prime factor other than \(2\) or \(5\), since that factor would remain in the product. The complete list of possible numbers from \(1\) through \(46\) is
\[
1,2,4,8,16,32,5,10,20,40,25.
\]
Indeed, these are the powers of \(2\), five times a power of \(2\), and \(25\); higher powers of \(5\) or \(2\cdot25\) exceed \(46\).

For a number \(2^a5^b\), call \(a-b\) its balance. A product is a power of \(10\) exactly when its total balance is zero. Only \(5\) and \(25\) have negative balances, namely \(-1\) and \(-2\). Only \(1\) and \(10\) have balance zero. Among the other numbers, \(2,20\) have balance \(1\), \(4,40\) have balance \(2\), and \(8,16,32\) have balances \(3,4,5\).

Both \(5\) and \(25\) must be selected. Otherwise, at most one negative balance and two zero balances would force at least three positive balances among the six numbers. Their sum would be at least \(3\), exceeding the available negative magnitude of at most \(2\).

These two selected numbers contribute total balance \(-3\). Both \(1\) and \(10\) must also be selected. If either were omitted, the remaining four numbers would include at least three positive balances. The three smallest available positive balances are \(1,1,2\), whose sum \(4\) is already too large.

The last two numbers must therefore have positive balances summing to \(3\), so one has balance \(1\) and the other balance \(2\). Every eligible ticket is consequently
\[
\{1,5,10,25,u,v\},
\quad u\in\{2,20\},\quad v\in\{4,40\}.
\]
All \(2\cdot2=4\) choices give six distinct permitted numbers and total balance zero. Different pairs \((u,v)\) give different unordered sets, so this count has neither omissions nor repetitions.

Conditioning on the winning ticket having the property leaves these four sets equally likely. Professor Gamble holds one of them, so his probability of winning is \(1/4\), choice B.

review.mathematicalCheck: The logarithm condition requires a product 2^k5^k. The listed eleven possible numbers are exhaustive. The balance bounds force inclusion of 5,25,1,10, leaving one choice from {2,20} and one from {4,40}. These give exactly four distinct valid sets. Under the explicitly stated fair-lottery model, their conditional probabilities are equal, yielding 1/4.
